event: USS Archerfish, under a captain who had once asked to be relieved for failing, chases the secret supercarrier Shinano through the night off Honshu and sinks her on her maiden voyage, the largest warship ever sunk by a submarine
place: Pacific Ocean south of Honshu, Japan, between Omaezaki and Cape Shiono
why: A failure and redemption arc (Enright asked to be relieved after a fruitless first patrol in Dace, then got a second chance), a six hour night chase told minute by minute in his own patrol report, a captain on the other side who asked for more time and was refused, the biggest ship ever sunk by a submarine, and the twist that the Navy first credited him with a carrier less than half her size; far beyond Spec Sheet No. 99.
alternates: HMT Rohna, 26 November 1943: a German Hs 293 radio guided glide bomb sinks the troopship off Algeria, killing 1,015 Americans, a loss kept quiet for decades (figures to verify if chosen).

The Cocoanut Grove nightclub fire in Boston, 28 November 1942: 492 dead, many of them servicemen on leave, a home front disaster that changed fire codes and burn treatment (figures to verify if chosen).

facts.text: Shinano's keel was laid on 4 May 1940 in the new Drydock No. 6 at Yokosuka, as hull No. 110, the third Yamato class battleship. After Japan lost four carriers at Midway in June 1942, the half built hull was redesigned as an aircraft carrier.

Her building was so secret that the Americans did not know what she was. On 16 August 1944 U.S. codebreakers read a Japanese telegram assigning men to the new ship Shinano and, because she was named for a river, guessed she was a cruiser.

On 1 November 1944 a B-29 photographed Shinano moored outside Yokosuka harbor. That growing enemy interest is why the navy decided to move her to Kure, the safer Inland Sea base, before her fitting out was finished.

Sources give different weights for her. Wikipedia, citing standard references, gives about 65,800 tonnes standard and 72,000 long tons at full load; the postwar JANAC list credits her at 59,000 tons standard; the Navy Cross citation says 72,000 tons. Either way she was the heaviest carrier built until the 1950s and remains the largest warship ever sunk by a submarine.
Shinano was commissioned at Yokosuka on 19 November 1944, under Capt. Toshio Abe, who had been in charge of her since August as chief fitting out officer.

On 27 November Abe asked to postpone the voyage for a few days so more work could be finished and the crew could train. The request was rejected: the danger of air raids on Yokosuka and the need for Ohka suicide planes in the Philippines both seemed urgent.

Shinano left Yokosuka on 28 November with the destroyers Hamakaze, Yukikaze and Isokaze, carrying 50 Ohka rocket bombs and six Shinyo suicide boats. Tully's record gives departure at 1:30 p.m. and the group clearing Tokyo Bay at 6:30 p.m.; other accounts put departure at about 6 p.m.
Only eight of her twelve boilers were finished and she sailed with six lit, enough for 24 knots. With no air cover available, Abe made the run by night.
Roughly 2,500 people were aboard: Wikipedia, citing Garzke and Dulin, gives a crew of 2,175 plus 300 shipyard workers and 40 civilian employees, and the New York Times put the total at 2,515.

Joseph Francis Enright was born in Minot, North Dakota, on 18 September 1910, graduated from the Naval Academy in 1933, served three years in the battleship Maryland, and joined the submarine force in 1936.

On 23 July 1943 Enright took command of the brand new submarine USS Dace. On her first war patrol that autumn he was sent an intelligence fix on the Japanese carrier Shokaku but could not get into attack position, and the carrier passed unharmed. The 49 day patrol sank nothing.

Back at Midway, Enright took the blame and asked to be relieved of command. Admiral Charles Lockwood agreed, and Enright spent about half a year on shore duty at the Midway submarine base before asking for another boat, a rare second chance.

He got it. On 29 September 1944, at Pearl Harbor, Cmdr. J. F. Enright relieved Cmdr. H. W. Wright as captain of USS Archer-Fish (SS-311), a Balao class boat built at Portsmouth Navy Yard and commissioned on 4 September 1943. She had a crew of about 81.

Archerfish left Pearl Harbor on 30 October 1944 for her fifth war patrol, in the waters south of Honshu. Besides hunting ships she was a lifeguard for the B-29 raids on Tokyo, standing by to rescue downed airmen.
At 8:48 p.m. on 28 November, Archerfish's radar picked up a contact at 24,700 yards. By 9:40 p.m. Enright had identified it as an aircraft carrier making about 20 knots and began a surface chase.

At 10:50 p.m. the carrier switched on a red masthead light for about ten seconds, off for twenty, on again for ten. Fearing gunfire, Enright sent his lookouts below and watched for flashes; the nearest escort, 6,100 yards away, kept ignoring him, so he called them back up.

Shinano's lookouts had in fact sighted the surfaced submarine at 10:45 p.m. Abe told his destroyers to hold fire. He believed a lone submarine in plain view was probably a decoy for a wolfpack and chose to turn away from it rather than attack.
Enright counted four escorts, one on each beam, one ahead and one astern. There were really three destroyers.

The carrier was about one knot faster than Archerfish at her best, but each zigzag gave the submarine a little ground. Then at 11:30 p.m. an overheated turbine on one of Shinano's shafts forced her down to 18 knots.
At 3:05 a.m. on 29 November, with the carrier turning toward him, Enright dived about 11,700 yards ahead of her. An escort passed only 400 yards ahead of the submarine without spotting it.

From 1,400 yards, Archerfish fired all six bow tubes, Mark 14 torpedoes set to run at 10 feet. Her log gives the time as 3:17 a.m.; the Japanese record gives the hits at 3:09; Wikipedia, citing Enright's book, has the firing at 3:15.

Enright saw the first hit near the stern, with a large ball of fire climbing the carrier's side, and a second about 50 yards forward of it. Diving away from a destroyer, the crew heard four more, and he claimed six certain hits. Japanese records count four, all on the starboard side, and the Navy Cross citation also says four.

Archerfish took 14 depth charges, the closest perhaps 300 yards away, between 3:25 and 3:45 a.m. Her sonar then heard hissing and breaking noises for 47 minutes. She escaped deep; the New York Times obituary gives 400 feet.

Enright guessed his target was about 750 feet long and looked like a Hayataka class carrier with a raked stern. Shinano was in fact about 872 feet (266 meters) long. In his report he hoped that a reconnaissance plane over Yokohama had a picture that could identify her.

At 3:34 a.m. Abe radioed that he had received an attack of four torpedoes. At first the damage looked manageable and he kept up speed and course, which forced more water in. Flooding spread through unfinished compartments that had never been air tested for leaks, as her executive officer later said.
By 6:00 a.m. the list had reached 18 degrees and the boilers were shut down. Shinano was dead in the water by 7:20. Hamakaze and Isokaze took her in tow at 8:50, but the cables parted.

Abe ordered abandon ship at 10:18 a.m. At 10:57 Shinano rolled over to starboard and sank stern first, less than a day after leaving Yokosuka and 10 days after commissioning. Archerfish, submerged miles away, logged a large distant explosion at 10:00 a.m. by her own clock.

Captain Abe went down with his ship by his own choice, along with 1,435 officers, men and civilians, among them the chief navigator and the chief gunnery officer. The destroyers rescued 1,080: 55 officers, 993 petty officers and men, and 32 civilians. Abe was promoted to rear admiral after his death.

The navy kept the loss quiet. Survivors were held on the island of Mitsuko-jima in Kure Bay until January 1945, and a court of inquiry under Vice Adm. Gunichi Mikawa blamed no one in particular, concluding that a gamble had been taken with an unfinished ship and lost.

U.S. naval intelligence doubted Enright's claim at first, since no one knew such a ship existed. On 23 December 1944 the Pacific submarine command credited Archerfish with one carrier, Hayataka type or possibly larger, of 28,000 tons: what Blair identifies as the Hiyo class. It accepted six hits.
After the war the truth came out. The 1947 JANAC report credits Archerfish with sinking the aircraft carrier Shinano, 59,000 tons, on 29 November 1944.

Enright received the Navy Cross, photographed at Pearl Harbor on 5 March 1945 just after the presentation. His citation, which by then gave the carrier's weight as 72,000 tons, credits him with six hours of determined chase. Archerfish received the Presidential Unit Citation for the patrol.
Shinano's sisters did not outlast her for long. Musashi had been sunk by U.S. carrier planes in the Sibuyan Sea on 24 October 1944, five weeks earlier, and Yamato was sunk in April 1945.
Archerfish was one of 12 U.S. submarines in Tokyo Bay for the Japanese surrender on 2 September 1945. Around then Enright went to see Dock No. 6 at Yokosuka, where Shinano had been built.

Enright retired as a captain in 1963 after commands including the cruiser Boston. In 1987 he published Shinano! The Sinking of Japan's Secret Supership, written with James W. Ryan (St. Martin's Press). He died at his home in Fairfax, Virginia, on 20 July 2000, aged 89, and is buried at Arlington.
